intro: Darwin is the capital of Australia's Northern Territory, a tropical harbour city rebuilt more than once after war and cyclone. In the city centre on Cavenagh Street, among glass and concrete, stands a boab with two swollen grey bottle trunks. A reader who sent us its photograph tells us it was planted in the late 1800s and marks the site of Darwin's first primary school. Their account is on the tree's page, in their own words.

trees.story:
A reader sent this boab from Cavenagh Street in the centre of Darwin, with a note that begins: “Standing proudly in the heart of Darwin, this heritage-listed Boab is much more than an impressive tree. Planted in the late 1800s, it marks the site of Darwin’s first primary school and has witnessed generations of Territory history, including the later Darwin High School and Adult Education Centre.”

They go on to say that during the Second World War an unexploded ‘Daisy Cutter’ bomb lay beneath its canopy for several days, and they give it a girth of 940 centimetres. These are the reader's facts, and we have not yet found the heritage listing they mention, so read them as theirs.

The photograph shows two swollen grey bottle trunks rising side by side out of a planted bed, each narrowing as it climbs, and above them a wide, airy crown of twigs coming into fresh green leaf. Paving runs round the bed, and the glass and concrete of the city stand close on both sides. The boab, Adansonia gregorii, is the baobab of northern Australia.

Look for the twin grey bottles among the buildings.
